questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why jellyfish numbers are falling in warmer seas
How to avoid getting stung by jellyfish on the beach
How jellyfish damage fishing boats and their nets
How jellyfish mucus could help remove ocean plastic
questions.why: Georgina says they'll learn how jellyfish mucus could provide the answer to plastic waste in the seas.

questions.q: Which problem caused by jellyfish is mentioned at the start?
options: Blocking pipes at power stations
Eating all the fish in the sea
Damaging coral reefs
Polluting drinking water
questions.why: Georgina says some species scare tourists, clog fishing nets and even block power station pipes.

questions.q: Where have microplastics been found, according to Neil?
options: Only in the water near big coastal cities
Only on beaches in Europe and North America
In Arctic ice, the seabed and inside humans
Mainly in rivers and lakes rather than the sea
questions.why: Neil says they have been found in Arctic ice, at the bottom of the sea and inside animals, including humans.

questions.q: What does Dr Rotter remember about her childhood?
options: Plastic bags were very cheap and everyone used them
They used cloth bags and almost no single-use plastic
The sea near her home was always full of jellyfish
Her family carefully recycled all of their plastic
questions.why: She says they always shopped with cloth bags and single-use spoons or forks were unheard of.

questions.q: How does the UN describe plastic pollution?
options: As a small local problem in a few countries
As a problem that has now largely been solved
As much less serious than overfishing or climate
As one of the world's top environmental threats
questions.why: Georgina says the UN lists plastic pollution as one of the world's top environmental threats.

questions.q: Why does Dr Rotter compare jellyfish mucus to a magnet?
options: Tiny plastic particles stick to it
It is made of metal
It pulls jellyfish towards the shore
It attracts fish for jellyfish to eat
questions.why: She says particles can attach to the mucus, so it could act as a magnet for microplastics.

questions.q: Why does Georgina say the idea 'couldn't have come at a better time'?
options: Plastic use around the world is falling quickly
Scientists have already finished all their research
Warmer seas and overfishing have boosted jellyfish
Tourists have stopped visiting beaches with jellyfish
questions.why: She says rising sea temperatures and overfishing of predators have boosted jellyfish numbers.

questions.q: What does Neil say about the state of Dr Rotter's research?
options: It is already cleaning the oceans
It is still at an early stage
It has been stopped because of costs
It has failed to find any results
questions.why: Neil says Dr Rotter's research is still in the early stages.
